title: Decouple dissector success from bytes dissected
description:
Define a value which a dissector can return if it did not process any
packet bytes, but was still "successful" in whatever manner.

As seen in [`packet.h`][1], a dissector's return value is nominally
expected to return a number of bytes greater than 0 if it was able to
dissect data, less than 0 if it needs a specific amount of extra data,
or 0 if it is explicitly rejecting the data. This patch postulates
another return value, the constant `DISSECT_OK_NO_DATA`, for when
a dissector is able to perform some analysis (and thus, should not be
removed from the list of protocols in this packet), while not consuming
any of the packet bytes.

The bulk of this patch is devoted to ensuring, as much as possible, that
everything will continue to work as expected when a dissector returns
this new value.

Motivation:
===========

When a dissector is called via `call_dissector_work()`, that function
[removes that protocol from the packet's protocol stack][2] if the
called dissector returns 0. This can interfere with taps, following
conversations, etc. when there is a valid reason for keeping that
protocol on the stack. See for example #15159.

Challenges:
===========

I found roughly 3500 uses of `call_dissector()`,
`dissector_try_someType()`, etc. In a large majority of cases,
a non-zero return was treated as "success" and a zero return as
"failure". Any non-zero value for `DISSECT_OK_NO_DATA` will allow this
use case to continue to function without change. (I chose this approach
in order to minimize the amount of affected code, even if it may not be
the "best" approach for decoupling success/failure from byte counts.)

Most of the changes in this patch are cases where the return value of
a dissector is used as a mathematical value for subsequent calculations.
Here I've attempted to respect the inferred use of the return value
(whether it's to indicate success/failure, or to count the number of
bytes processed) while adding checks for `DISSECT_OK_NO_DATA`.

Notes:
======

I have not changed any dissector to return `DISSECT_OK_NO_DATA`.

It is a conscious decision to explicitly test for this constant, rather
than grouping it into a pre-existing inequality test (`<`/`>`). The
constant indicates a specific requirement to *not* perform math on the
result. Conversely, tests for zero/nonzero are left unmodified, as
described above.

There is much logic in Wireshark which assumes that a nonzero dissector
return value must be positive by definition. My changes only add the
`DISSECT_OK_NO_DATA` check; that is, I *do not* add checks for negative
values. Even if there is code which should perform that test, it would
be out of scope for this change.

[1]:
https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/ec353e89f321487dfad19d4dcf1d68ff38d47a0f/epan/packet.h#L64-75
[2]:
https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/ec353e89f321487dfad19d4dcf1d68ff38d47a0f/epan/packet.c#L922-938

Fixes #12368

notes.body: It might be cleaner, if more work to implement, if there were a `PACKET_NOT_OURS` return value, with a return value of 0 meaning "this packet is mine, but the only information in it for me is data passed on from the previous layer, or found by request/response matching, or..., so I didn't dissect anything from the payload".
Agreed. I don't know what's best for the project, I'm just starting with a small change to see what conversation it sparks.
Other approaches to this problem would be better in their own MRs, so I'm calling this discussion resolved.

10 months without comment or merging is a pretty clear message. Nudging on Discord prompted this response, which makes the message explicit:

> For me, overloading the return value, which requires additional handling (see most of your changes), together with the prospect of the need to have more conditions handled in the future, together with the still ongoing change of dissectors from returning true/false to 'bytes consumed', together with required changes to code generators, makes me hold back on going this route.

So, I'm closing this MR.

(IMHO this approach requires the *least* amount of additional handling, compared to other approaches floated by Guy. But I'm not privy to the bigger picture the core developers have for the codebase.)
